Hayyotze miggevul haemori. retzua yotzea miggevul haemori vehi shel emoriyyim, venichneset ligvul moav ad arnon shehu gevul moav, vesham chanu yishorael velo vau ligvul moav, ki aranon gabol moab, vehem lo natenu lahem reshut laavor beartzam, veaapi shello fereshah moshe, pereshah yiftach, kemo sheamar yiftach (Shoftim 11) "vegam el melech moav shalach velo ava", umoshe remazah (Devarim 2), "kaasher asu li bene esav hayyoshevim beseir vehammoavim hayyoshevim bear" — ma ellu lo netanum laavor betoch artzam ella hikkifum saviv, af moav ken:

Veeshed hannechalim. targum shel shefech "eshed" — shefech hannechalim shennishpach sham dam emoriyyim, shehayu nechbaim sham, lefi shehayu heharim gevohim vehannachal amok vekatzar veheharim semuchim ze laze — adam omed al hahar mizze umedabber im chavero bahar hazze — vehadderech over betoch hannachal, ameru emoriyyim, kesheyyikkanesu yisrael laaretz letoch hannachal laavor, netze min hammearot shebbeharim shellemala mehem, venahargem bechitztzim veavne balisetraot, vehayu otan hannekaim bahar shel tzad moav, uvahar shel tzad emoriyyim hayu keneged otan nekaim kemin keranot veshadayim boletin lachutz, kevan shebbau yisrael laavor, nizdaza hahar shel eretz yisrael keshifcha hayyotzet lehakbil pene gevirtah, venitkarev letzad hahar shel moav venichnesu otan hashadayim letoch otan nekaim vaharagum, vezehu asher nata leshevet ar — shehahar nata mimmekomo venitkarev letzad moav venidbak bo, vezehu venishan ligvul moav (Tanchuma; Berachot 54):

Umisham beera. misham ba haeshed el habbeer; ketzad? amar hakkabbah mi modia levanay hannissim hallalu? hammashal omer "natatta pat letinok hodia leimmo". leachar sheaveru chazeru heharim limkomam, vehabbeer yorda letoch hannachal veheelta misham dam haharugim uzeroot veevarim umolachtan saviv hammachane, veyisrael rau veameru shira:
Beer chafaruha. zot hi habbeer asher chafaruha sarim — moshe veaharon:
Bemishanotam. bammatte:
Umimmidbar. nittena lahem:
Umimmattana nachaliel. ketargumo:

Umibbamot haggay asher bisde moav. ki sham met moshe vesham botla habbeer; daa, karuha nedive haam — kol nasi venasi keshehayu chonim notel maklo umoshech etzel diglo umachanehu, ume habbeer nimshachin derech oto siman uvain lifne chaniyyat kol shevet vashevet (tanchuma):

Bamachakak. al pi moshe shennikra mechokek, shenneemar "ki sham chelkat mechokek safun" (Devarim 33); velamma lo nizkar moshe beshira zo? lefi shellaka al yede habbeer, vechevan shello nizkar shemo shel moshe lo nizkar shemo shel hakkabbah, mashal lemelech shehayu mezammenin oto lisuda, amar im ohavi sham ani sham, veim lav eni holech (tanchuma):
Rosh happisga. ketargumo "resh ramata":
Pasagah. leshon govah, vechen "passegu armenoteha" (Tehillim 48) — hagbihu armenoteha:

Venishkafa. otah happisga al pene hammakom sheshemo yeshimon, vehu leshon midbar shehu shamem; davar acher venishkafa habbeer al pene hayshimon, shennigneza beyammah shel teverya, vehaomed al hayshimon mabbit veroe kemin kevara bayyam, vehi habbeer, kach darash rabbi tanchuma:

Vayyishlach yisrael malachim. uvemakom acher tole hashelichut bemoshe, shenneemar "vaeshlach malachim mimmidbar kedemot" (Devarim 2), vechen "vayyishlach moshe malachim mikkadesh el melech edom" (Bamidbar 20), uveyiftach hu omer (Shoftim 11) "vayyishlach yisrael malachim el melech edom" vego', hakketuvim hallalu tzerichin ze laze, ze noel veze foteach, shemmoshe hu yisrael veyisrael hem moshe, lomar lecha shennesi haddor hu kechol haddor, ki hannasi hu hakkol (tanchuma):
Ebera veartzecha. aapi shello nitztavvu liftoach lahem beshalom bikkeshu mehem shalom (sham):

Velo natan sichon vegomer'. lefi shekkol malche chenaan hayu maalin lo mas, shehaya shomeram shello yaavru alehem geyasot, kevan sheameru lo yisrael ebera veartzecha, ala, kol atzmi eni yoshev kan ella leshomram mippenechem, veattem omerim kach (tanchuma):

Vayyetze likrat yisrael. illu hayeta cheshbon melea yattushin en kol beriyya yechola lechovshah, veim haya sichon bichfar challash en kol adam yachol lechovsho, vechol shekken shehaya becheshbon; amar hakkabbah ma ani matriach al banay kol zot latzur al kol ir vair? natan belev kol anshe hammilchama latzet min haayarot, venitkabbetzu chullam lemakom echad vesham nafelu, umisham halechu yisrael el hearim veen omed lenegdam, ki en sham ella nashim vataf (sham):
Ki az. umahu chozko? hatraato shel hakkabbah sheamar lahem al tetzurem vego' (Devarim 2):
Benoteha. kefarim hassemuchim lah:

Vehu nilcham. lamma hutzrach likkatev? lefi shenneemar (sham) "al tatzar et moav", vecheshbon mishel moav hayeta, katav lanu shessichon lekachah mehem veal yado tahara leyishorael (Chullin 60; Gittin 38):
Miyyado. mereshuto (Bava Metzia 56):
Al ken. al otah milchama shennilcham sichon bemoav:
Yomru hammoshelim. bilam, shenneemar bo "vayyissa meshalo" (Bamidbar 23):
Hammoshelim. bilam uveor, vehem ameru:
Bou cheshbon. shello haya sichon yachol lechovshah vehalach vesachar et bilam lekallelo (tanchuma); vezehu sheamar lo balak "ki yadati et asher tevarech mevorach" vego' (Bamidbar 22):
Tibbane vetikkonen. cheshbon beshem sichon lihyot iro:
Ki esh yotza mecheshbon. mishekkevashah sichon:
Ochla ar moav. shem otah hammedina karuy ar belashon ivri ulechayat belashon arammi:
Ar moav. ar shel moav:
Oy lecha moav. shekkillelu et moav sheyyimmaseru veyado (tanchuma):
Kemosh. shem elohe moav:
Natan. hannoten et banav shel moav:
Peletim — nasim ufeletim mecherev veet benotav bashevit vego':
Vanniram avad. malchut shellahem:

Avad cheshbon ad divon — malchut veol shehaya lemoav becheshbon avad misham, vechen ad divon; targum shel sar "ad", kelomar sar nir middivon; nir leshon malchut veol memshelet ish, kemo "lemaan heyot nir ledavid avdi" (41 11):
Vannashim. shin degusha, leshon shemama, kach yomru hammoshelim, "vannashim otam ad nofach" — hashimmonum ad nofach:
Vayyishlach moshe leraggel et yazer. hamraggelim lechaduha, ameru lo naase karishonim, betuchim anu bechoach tefillato shel moshe lehillachem (tanchuma):

El tira oto. shehaya moshe yare lehillachem, shemma taamod lo zechuto shel avraham, shenneemar "vayyavo happalit" (Bereshit 14) — hu og sheppalat min harefaim shehikku kedorlaomer vachaverav beashterot karnayim, shenneemar (Devarim 3) "rak og melech habbashan nishar miyyeter harefaim" (nidda sa):
Vayyakku oto. moshe harago, kidita vivrachot beharoe (Berachot Daf 54), akar tura bar telata farse vechu':

Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:19-: And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b) it says: we have learned, there are two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled when it is defiled, meaning that it is [made ready] to be defiled - and therefore, "your camp shall be holy" - what is "your camp"? These are the limbs of the body. "That He see no ervat davar among you" - what is "ervat davar"? The nakedness of this "davar" - an allusion, as we have established, and so on - to this point. And the rest of the teaching we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 5 - see there.

And when we combine the two teachings, our intent emerges clearly explained - that according to all explanations, "your camp shall be holy" refers to the two hundred forty-eight limbs, and therefore "your camp" is mentioned in the plural form, to indicate the two hundred forty-eight limbs. And what is said in Parashat Noach, that "ervat davar" is the nakedness of speech, and what is said in Parashat Acharei Mot, that "ervat davar" is the Shechinah, are all one - for whoever blemishes the nakedness of speech blemishes her, since speech is from her - and this is what the teaching (in Parashat Noach) began with, saying "for YHVH your God walks [feminine form]" - this is the female.

And of necessity we must say, according to our approach, that "your camp shall be holy," referring to the two hundred forty-eight, [means] that "walks in the midst of your camp" also refers to the camp of the body - for the totality of the two hundred forty-eight is one camp in which the soul rests, and the soul, since it comes from the Atzilut of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and it walks within the body - the soul has no life to produce the power of speech except according to how the Shechinah bestows it, for the soul is a thread drawn from above from these two measures, as it says (Deuteronomy 32:9), "for the LORD's portion is His people" - and it is impossible to separate the portion from its root. It follows that since the soul is below, that "YHVH your God" is literally "walks in the midst of your camp," and this is "YHVH your God" - the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, from whom is the emanation of the soul, and they are voice and speech.

And the reason it says "mit'halech" [feminine] and not "mehalech" [masculine] is because the essential thing in man is speech, and voice is secondary to it, therefore it says "mit'halech" [feminine, matching speech/the Shechinah]. And likewise, the place of the soul's gestation is within her, and she is the mother who bears it, and she raises the children - therefore she is the essential thing in this matter. And therefore it says, "that He see no ervat davar among you" - meaning, the Shechinah, who walks within you, along the lines explained, that she is the soul, and so on, should not see [him make] her power go out in vain, to a place of nakedness, namely speech. And therefore it says that "ervat dibbur" [nakedness of speech] is more despised than anything, because it is a blemish in the Shechinah and in the soul, though only in a spiritual aspect - for speech is more spiritual than deed, as explained above concerning "who is the man who desires life."

And it says "your camp shall be holy" - that the two hundred forty-eight limbs be on the side of holiness and not be defiled - as it says in Parashat Acharei Mot, "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled" - and there is no sin that defiles all two hundred forty-eight limbs like the sin of seminal emission, for the seed emerges from all his two hundred forty-eight limbs, and all of them are defiled by the spirit of impurity from Lilith resting upon him. And through this the matter "that He see no ervat davar among you" is precisely understood - meaning, He shall not see, in your body, a nakedness of speech - for when the Shechinah is blemished, which you have blemished, the blemish in her shows in your body, and the nakedness, which is Lilith, "ervat davar," rests upon you, and then the Shechinah withdraws from you, and this is "and turn away from you," for "evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5).

And there is proof for this explanation in Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Zavim (18:4): where were Israel obligated in flux [zivah] and leprosy? Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya said, because they would slander their leaders, saying, this family of so-and-so is not free of leprosy - to teach you that plagues come only because of slander. Rabbi Tanchuma said, because they would slander the Ark, saying, this Ark kills its bearers - and plagues come only because of slander - therefore Israel became obligated in flux and leprosy - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that flux came to them through the blemish of slander. And flux blemishes the covenant, and my teacher, peace be upon him, explained that "zav" [flux] totals nine, for its blemish is in the Righteous One [Yesod], the ninth attribute - and likewise concerning seminal emission, whose blemish is in the covenant, as we shall elaborate in its place - its cause shall be the blemish of the tongue, through slander and the other things that blemish the tongue.

And so it is explained in Parashat Metzora (page 53a), whose wording we shall copy below: Rabbi Chiya said, whoever utters slander, all his limbs become defiled, and so on - and this is along the lines of "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled," as explained.

Further, it is possible to explain "that He see no ervat davar among you" as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso, page 121b), close to the previous approach, in these words: come and see, at the time people sleep and taste the taste of death, and the soul ascends above, it stands in the place it stands, and is examined concerning its deeds performed that whole day, and they write it on a note - why? Because the soul ascends above and testifies concerning a person's deeds and concerning every single word emerging from his mouth, because that word a person utters from his mouth ascends and splits the firmaments, and stands in the place it stands, until night enters and the soul ascends and takes hold of that word and brings it before the King - this is what is written (Micah 7:5), "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom" - and then that word and that sin are marked upon the person, and therefore (Psalms 32:2), "happy is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity" - when? When there is no deceit in his spirit - to this point.

Behold, it says "that word and that sin are marked upon the person," and it is explained by what is known, that some sins are marked and written on the skin of the flesh of the face, and some on the forehead, and some are engraved on his bones, as they explained, of blessed memory - and this is "marked upon the person" - literally upon him is marked the sin of that speech.

And even though he performed no deed, nevertheless speech is more severe than deed, as explained in the Mishnah (Arachin, chapter 3, mishnah 5) - it is found that one who says with his mouth is [more culpable] than one who performs a deed, for we find that the decree against our forefathers in the wilderness was not sealed except because of slander, as it is said (Numbers 14:22), "and have tested Me [with their words]." And we learn from this, that if he thought in his mind to commit a transgression and decided in his mind to do it, and uttered that decision with his lips, it is accounted before Him, blessed be He, as though he did it, for speech is accounted like a deed, as they said in the Mishnah. And they said, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 40a), only that a person who thought to commit a transgression and did not commit it, it is not accounted to him, is when he did not speak - and this is (Psalms 66:18), "if I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the LORD would not have heard" - but if I spoke with my lips, the LORD would hear. And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Emor, page 105a) concerning speech on the Sabbath, that speech is forbidden because the voice immediately ascends above, but lustful thought is permitted. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Idra of Ha'azinu (page 294a), in the repair of the ears - see there. And so it is explained in the previous chapter on the verse "do not be rash with your mouth," and so on - see there.

And through this "that He see no ervat davar among you" is understood - meaning that the nakedness of that speech is imprinted and marked in his body, and this is "bach" [in you] - literally, in your body it is marked - and once the body is blemished by transgression, it is blemished, and the Shechinah withdraws from it - and this is "and turn away from you," for "whoever has a blemish shall not approach" (Leviticus 21:18).

Further, it is possible to explain "that He see no [unseemly thing] among you" [bach] along the lines explained in the Zohar (Zohar Chadash, Shir HaShirim, page 68a) concerning "let us be glad and rejoice in you [bach]" (Song of Songs 1:4), that "bach" is the twenty-two letters, and "bach" is Tiferet. And it is known that the twenty-two letters of the Torah are marked in a person's mouth, as explained above concerning "do not be rash with your mouth," which are Alef-Chet-Heh-Ayin in the throat, and so on - and it means, "He shall not see 'bach'" - He shall not see the Torah, which is fixed in your mouth in the twenty-two letters, [if] you utter its letters for speech of nakedness - for it is found that you blemish the five supernal points of articulation, which are the source of the twenty-two letters. And when he considers where the supernal allusion of each and every point of articulation is, he shall see how great is the blemish of the tongue - and the allusion is seen in a person's mouth, in that he has thirty-two teeth, corresponding to the thirty-two paths of Chokhmah, which are the thirty-two [mentions of] "Elohim" in the account of creation - and this is one of the points of articulation, Zayin-Tzadi-Samech-Resh-Shin, in the teeth, and likewise the other points of articulation, Alef-Chet-Heh-Ayin in the throat - the throat being more internal, the blemish there is greater, and likewise for the other points of articulation - it follows that the blemish is in all of them together. And therefore it says, "that He see no 'bach'" - meaning the twenty-two letters that are in the five points of articulation - "ervat davar," that a blemish of the nakedness of speech be found in them. And this is also the secret of Tiferet, called "bach," which comprises the twenty-two letters of the Torah - He shall see no "ervat davar," which is His Shechinah - for when He sees the Shechinah blemished, He withdraws, and this is "and turn away from you," from which it follows that mercy withdraws from him, along the lines explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 5.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:31-: Now, from all the explanations set forth on this verse, we can understand what the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 17), "all my days I grew up among the Sages, and I found nothing," and so on. And the explanation of "all my days I grew up" is that a person, according to the place he grows up in, learns qualities, whether for good or the opposite - and therefore he says that he grew up among the Sages, and what he learned from them is that he found nothing better than silence - and among the Sages this quality must necessarily be found, for they said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 7), "seven things characterize a sage," and so on: "a sage does not speak in the presence of one greater than him in wisdom, and does not interrupt his fellow's words" - and the root of all the other qualities mentioned concerning a sage is silence.

"I have found nothing better for the body than silence" - what is the matter of "the body"? Let it say, "I have found nothing better than silence"? Rather, the matter, according to our explanation, that the two hundred forty-eight limbs are defiled - it means, I have found no better purity for the body than silence - and support for this explanation I found in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 16:5), which we copied in chapter 13, on "cause your flesh to sin" - do not give permission to one of your limbs to cause all your limbs to sin. Or, according to the explanation that the blemish is marked in his body - if he does not sin with his mouth and stays silent, certainly that sin will not be marked in his body, and likewise mercy will not withdraw from him.

Or it is possible to say, "I have found nothing for the body" - meaning, for the affairs of the body, silence is good, but for words of Torah one must speak, along the lines of "silence of righteousness" explained above. Further, it means "for the body," along the lines explained in the Midrash concerning (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" - the parable of the lion cub they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Tehillim, remez 721).

Further, I found in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, that a certain man, after he passed away, was found by the gravediggers in his grave still alive, for the worm had not ruled over him, and Rav Nachman asked him what merit brought him this - and he answered that he had no envy and did not incline his ear to hear idle words - and we copied this teaching in the Gate of Humility, chapter 3, and at the end of the teaching it says, and this one, who had nothing but the reward of silence alone, and so on.

And in Sefer Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, another explanation is given, in these words: I have found no remedy for the body but silence, for whoever multiplies words is not saved from sin, and shall be afflicted with leprosy in his body. And in light of what Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, Parashat Mishpatim, page 122a), in these words: we have learned, it is written (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil [mera]" - what is "mera"? Because of slander, illnesses [mar'in] descend to the world - to this point - we shall explain, "I have found nothing for the body" that would be saved from evil illnesses - not specifically leprosy, as he explains, but all illnesses - "but silence," through which he is saved - and this is a great virtue of silence.

And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Metzora 16:5): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a word is worth a sela, silence two - for we have learned, his son Shimon says, all my days I grew up among the Sages and found nothing better for the body than silence - to this point. And through this explanation, two precise points that need examining in the Mishnah are resolved: the first, why it enters into a negative formulation; the second, the word "better" [tov] - for one does not say "this is better than that" unless they are in the same category and of equal standing, and then one says "this is better than that." And through this everything is resolved - for it comes to teach us that a word is worth a sela, silence worth two - and this is what it says, "I have found nothing for the body better than silence" - that even though speech is worth a sela, silence is better than it and worth two - and it does not, by this, exclude silence from idle talk, slander, and the like, for in these speech is not good at all, so that we could say silence is better than speech - and there is no equivalence in selas for them, for on the contrary, they are blemishing.

And the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote in his commentary on this Mishnah, in these words: and one who refrains from speaking where he has need to speak indicates three things about his soul: the first, that he is knowledgeable, since he is not rash to speak, meaning, "an empty jug clatters" [i.e., he is not empty]; the second, that his intellect overpowers his materiality and therefore he restrains his words; the third, that he is understanding and his eyes are in his head, to see the harm fitting to come from his words - and this is what Solomon said (Proverbs 17:27), "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable; a man of understanding has a cool spirit" - in saying "restrains," it teaches that he has need to speak and even so restrains himself, for this is the common usage of the term - "and I too withheld [va'echsoch]" (Genesis 20:6), "he has withheld [lo chasach] nothing from me" (ibid. 39:9) - and so Rabbi Yosef ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory, wrote, and he is described with three descriptions: "knowledgeable," "of cool spirit," "a man of understanding" - to this point.

And it appears to me that these three descriptions correspond to Chokhmah, Binah, Da'at, and it begins with Da'at, which is the essence of the tongue, and afterward "yekar ru'ach" [cool/precious spirit], which is the honor of the heart from Chokhmah, from where the spirit of life flows, [then] "a man of understanding" corresponding to Binah - and because he holds the place of life, as explained concerning "who is the man who desires life," it is fitting that he be described by these three.

And the Tanna connected to this, saying, "not the exposition is the essential thing, but the deed." It is possible to connect his words in two ways: the first, that he comes to tell us that having taught us this good quality, that he found nothing better for the body than silence, his students afterward, when they cite this quality, should not intend only to study it and not practice it, so that it be found "attractive in teaching but not attractive in practice," but rather that they practice and acquire the quality of silence - and the same applies to all matters a person is called to practice, that not the exposition is the essential thing. And the reason he taught us this matter concerning the tongue is that a person's acquisition of this quality requires great effort, because of the habit of the tongue and its swiftness to speak good and evil - and whoever fulfills this quality shall have a key to acquiring all the other good qualities that exist, and it is well for him to study and practice, for once he has grasped his root and guarded it properly, all the branches shall endure.

Further, it means that he comes to resolve a difficulty - for it is fitting to ask, what does he come to teach us, that silence is good, when in several verses from the words of King Solomon, peace be upon him, the matter of silence is already mentioned - "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable" (Proverbs 17:27), "therefore let your words be few" (Ecclesiastes 5:1), and many similar ones? To this he says, "not the exposition is the essential thing" - meaning, my intent in saying "I have found nothing better for the body than silence" is that I read the words of Solomon and fulfilled them - and so it is fitting for everyone who reads the words of King Solomon, peace be upon him, to fulfill them.

And the same applies to all matters where "not the exposition is the essential thing," and so on, but this is a key to them. And the reason is that whoever accustoms himself to silence and not uttering a word in vain, out of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, who are the inwardness of the soul, being voice and speech, shall gain from this the intent in his prayer, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (page 3a), that one must direct his intent, in every place and every utterance, [that] voice and speech are the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and so on.

And since he has trained himself in worldly matters not to utter voice and speech in vain, all the more so shall he not utter them in vain in his prayer - and therefore they established, at the end [of the Amidah], "my God, guard my tongue from evil" - and the intent, as explained above, is that one who utters a word in vain is like one who emits seed in vain, who is called "ra" - and if a person guards himself in worldly matters from uttering a word in vain, all the more so in his prayer; and if, Heaven forfend, he is blemished in his tongue, his prayer does not ascend above, for it is subdued under that side, as explained in Parashat Pekudei (page 263b), whose wording we shall copy below in chapter 13 concerning blemish.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:43-: And so it brings him to humility and fear together, when he considers what we explained on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:1), "and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God" - that when he considers that he stands before the blessed Name, he should not answer his own disgrace, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 38:16), "for in You, O LORD, I hope" - and this is "my soul shall be silent," and so on - and his voice shall be low, for he shall be ashamed to raise his voice before the King. And in considering always that his soul cleaves to its root, he shall strive to occupy himself with Torah and commandments for the honor of his Father and Mother and to do their will, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 146b), concerning (Exodus 20:12), "honor your father and your mother," which we copied in the Gate of Love. And he shall likewise strive not to cause any blemish, for in blemishing he blemishes the supernal roots. And this matter shall cause him to repent of all his sins, in order to purify his soul so that it cleave to its root. And it causes him to purify his thoughts, for he shall be ashamed to think something against His blessed service, because the blessed Name watches, being within him, along the lines explained. And since he cleaves to the Tree of Life, he shall be strong in trust that nothing of worldly matters shall harm him, and that he is forever watched over from above, as it is said (Psalms 33:18), "behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear Him," and so on. It follows that the acquisition of this measure is the root for the fulfillment of the whole Torah, since he knows it in its secret, as explained, and shall fulfill it.

And further, concerning the virtue of silence, what the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 13), "a fence for wisdom is silence" - the explanation is that just as tithes are a fence for wealth - for in order to attain wealth one must tithe, as explained (Shabbat 119a), "you shall surely tithe" (Deuteronomy 14:22) - tithe so that you become wealthy - and so likewise the other fences mentioned in the Mishnah are along these lines - so, for a person to attain wisdom, it is impossible except through acquiring the measure of silence. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:21), that when a Torah scholar speaks an idle word, words of Torah go out from him in reaction - and we shall copy their wording in the next chapter. And along these lines it is possible to say the reason is that through his silence he removes himself from the actions of the six extremities, which are voice and speech, and ascends to the place of silence, which is thought, the secret of Chokhmah - as they said (Menachot 29b), "be silent, so it arose in thought."

And further, concerning the reason for the matter, since a person is silent he makes himself a chariot for the place of silence, and shall merit that the secrets of Torah, which are in silence, not handed over to be revealed, be flowed to him, as they said in the Zohar several times (Parashat Emor, page 105b). And one of the forty-eight things through which Torah is acquired is minimal conversation, and so on (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 6).

And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Midrash Yelamdenu, said concerning the matter of "and Miriam and Aaron spoke" (Numbers 12:1) - this is what Scripture says (Proverbs 10:19), "in the multitude of words, transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise" - whoever restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow is wise. Rabban Gamliel said, all my days I grew up among the Sages and found nothing better for the body than silence. Our Rabbis said, two rhetoricians stood before Hadrian - one of them was teaching that speech is good, and one was teaching about silence. The one said to him, my lord, there is nothing better than speech - were it not for speech, how would brides be praised, how would there be commerce in the world, how would ships set sail on the sea? He immediately said to the one who was teaching about the goodness of silence - he immediately began to speak. The one who had been teaching about speech stood up and slapped him. The king said to him, why did you slap him? He said to him, what I taught was about speech concerning speech, and this one comes to teach my proverb about his own [i.e., about silence, using speech]. Solomon said: the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute, but rather "and he who restrains his lips" from speaking about his fellow - pay attention that you not be punished. You have none greater than Aaron and Miriam - the well ascended and watered Israel by the merit of Miriam, and the clouds of glory surrounded Israel by the merit of Aaron - and since they gave their mouths permission and spoke about Moses, I did not stay silent toward them - to this point.

At first glance this teaching disagrees with the words of Rabbi Yitzchak that we copied in the previous chapter, who said (Chullin 89a), "what is a person's craft in this world? Let him make himself as one silent [mute]," as it is said (Psalms 58:1), "do you indeed [speak] in silence, O mighty ones" - while this teaching says that the matter of silence is [only] "he restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow," implying that everything else, a person is permitted to lengthen his tongue concerning his affairs and his business dealings and the like.

It may be said that when we examine his words precisely, that "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute, but rather 'he who restrains his lips,'" and so on, we find him a man of peace with us, and he does not disagree at all with the words of Rabbi Yitzchak.

And the matter is that Midrash Yelamdenu comes to explain the verse, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise" - for it is impossible to explain that Solomon's words go from one extreme to the other, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease," and "he who restrains his lips" referring to complete silence, which is the final extreme - rather, "he who restrains his lips" is the middle measure, restraining his lips from speaking about his fellow. And the word "restrains his lips" - it appears that although there is some benefit to speaking, nevertheless it is better not to speak - for Miriam intended for the sake of Heaven, to be fruitful and multiply, as we shall copy the teaching of the Sifrei below, and even so she was punished - and this is "restrains," in a place where there is [some justification] to speak. And nevertheless, reason dictates that if he is compelled to speak concerning matters of buying and selling, he should speak - and therefore it says, "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute" - lest a person say, since "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease," and the transgression certainly refers to speaking about one's fellow and the like, I shall sit like a deaf-mute so as not to come to this, and cease from dealing with people - and to this Solomon comes and says, "and he restrains his lips" from speaking about his fellow, to correct what he said at the beginning of the verse, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease" - for this he is called "wise" [maskil], having the sense to speak where it is fitting to speak, and his intellect overpowers his inclination and prevents him from where it is not fitting to speak. And further, it is possible that he is called "maskil" because speech is in the place of the female, and above her is (Psalms 89:1), "maskil of Eitan the Ezrachite," and so on, as explained in the Sabba (Parashat Mishpatim, pages 110a-b) - and the difference between male and female is that matters depend on it in intellect, in concealment, while in the female they are in speech, meaning in revelation - and since he is called "maskil," happy is he, for he is among those of whom it is said (Daniel 12:3), "and the wise [maskilim] shall shine like the brightness of the firmament," as they elaborated in the Tikkunim in manuscript, that no secret is withheld from them.

And there is a third division, which is silence concerning matters where one does not speak about his fellow, such as lengthening speech in stories of kings and parables of common people, and similarly lengthening speech in what is not absolutely necessary for his business dealings - since there is no benefit in these, one need not say "restrains," as explained, but it is certainly forbidden, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 1:8), "all things are wearisome; man cannot speak [of them all]," as shall be explained below. And King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned this division explicitly in the verse (Proverbs 17:27), "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable" - and the pious one, of blessed memory, explained that "restrains his words" means that he has need to speak, and even so restrains himself, as we copied his wording above - and he bases this on the verse (ibid. 17:28), "even a fool who keeps silent is thought wise; he who shuts his lips is deemed understanding" - and certainly the words "keeps silent" and "shuts" cannot be explained as referring to remaining silent or shutting his lips from speaking about his fellow, for this is not mentioned in the verse, and if this were the intent, why would King Solomon, peace be upon him, repeat his words, since it was already said above, "and he restrains his lips, is wise"? Rather, certainly he comes to teach us the matter that Rabbi Akiva said in the Mishnah, "a fence for wisdom is silence" - for even in what pertains to his own needs, he must be silent - meaning that he should not prolong his speech, and a matter that appears to him to have some justification for speaking and some justification for not speaking, not being so necessary, it is better not to speak - and this is what is said in the Midrash, "a word is worth a sela, silence worth two" - and the reason is that the measure of silence is in the measure of Chokhmah, as explained, and this is (Proverbs 17:28), "a fool who keeps silent is thought wise" - for he has grasped the measure of Chokhmah, as we elaborated above in the secret of speech. But whoever prolongs his words in worldly matters holds fast to Malchut, which conducts the world, where speech is - namely, "ten measures of conversation descended to the world, nine were taken by women" (Kiddushin 49b) - and this is the aspect of the Shechinah nesting in a manner (cf. Tikkunei Zohar, page 23a) so that he not become wise.

And there is an aspect of blemished speech corresponding to "Asiyah," where the husks are, such as slander, gossip, idle words, and the like - and therefore it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:8), "whoever breaches a fence, a serpent shall bite him" - for he breaches the fences of the walls of the tongue, just as the serpent forever stands among the fences and breached the fence of the world, as they explained, of blessed memory (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:2): Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said, they asked the serpent, why are you found among the fences? It said to them, because I breached the fence of the world. They said to it, why is your tongue on the ground? It said to them, this is what caused me, for I spoke slander against my Creator. And what slander did it speak? Rabbi Yehudah of Sichnin said in the name of Reish Lakish: the first serpent would converse like a human being - since Adam and Eve did not wish to eat from that tree, it began to speak slander against its Creator, saying to them, from this tree the Creator ate and created His world, and He commanded you not to eat from it so that you not create worlds like His. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He cut off its legs, and cut off its tongue so that it not converse. They asked the serpent, what pleasure do you get when you bite? It said to them, instead of asking me, ask the master of slander, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 10:11), "if the serpent bites without a charm, there is no advantage to the charmer" - what pleasure does he get when he speaks slander? They said to the serpent, why do you bite in one limb while your venom travels through all the limbs? It said to them, why do you ask me? Ask the master of slander, who speaks slander in Rome and kills in Syria - to this point, their wording. It follows that the master of the tongue is likened to the serpent in all his aspects - it follows that he descends to the place of the husks and breaches the fences of holiness and lets the external force enter, as shall be further explained in the sin of slander.

And what emerges from the sum of this chapter is that guarding the tongue from everything that blemishes it is needed, whether from slander, from vulgarity, or from idle words. And we have elaborated on the virtue of silence, because since a person is distinguished, through his speech, from beasts and animals, and is made equal to the angels, it is fitting to sanctify his speech, as it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachot, chapter 9, halachah 5), "all chatter is bad except the chatter of Torah, which is good." And it further says in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachot, chapter 1, halachah 2), Rabbi Levi said, had I been at Mount Sinai I would have asked for two mouths - for the mouth, which is fitting to speak words of Torah and praise and thanksgiving, should not speak worldly matters, all the more so if it be something blemishing.

And man's mouth was created for nothing other than to occupy itself with Torah, as we read in the chapter "Chelek" (Sanhedrin 99b): Rabbi Elazar says, man was created for toil, but I do not know if for the toil of his mouth or for another toil - when it says (Proverbs 16:26), "for his mouth compels him," it must be said that the mouth was created for toil - but I still do not know if for the toil of Torah or for the toil of conversation - when it says (Joshua 1:8), "this book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth," it must be said that it was created for the toil of Torah - to this point.

And one of the authors who writes on matters of piety speaks well concerning the matter of silence, and I saw fit to copy his words, in these words: and there was a story of Rabban Gamliel, who prepared a feast and told his servant to prepare several kinds of foods, and gave him money to buy the needs of the feast. The servant went and bought several tongues, and made some of them roasted and some cooked, some soft and some hard. He brought before them the cooked ones and then brought the roasted ones; he brought before them the soft ones and then brought before them the hard ones. Rabban Gamliel called the servant and said to him, what did you see, to do this - that some are hard and some are soft, and also roasted and cooked? He said to him, to let you know that everything is in the hand of the tongue - for sometimes it is good and soft, and sometimes it is evil or hard; if a person wishes, he does good with it, and if a person wishes, he does evil with it.

And there was a story of a certain king who had several advisors, wise, understanding, and knowledgeable men. Once the king saw that one of them, the wisest among them, was sitting silent and quiet. The king said to him, what is this, that you are so silent? He said to him, I have examined matters and found that they divide into four parts: the first entirely harmful; the second, harmful from one side and beneficial from another; the third, neither harmful nor beneficial; the fourth, entirely beneficial. The first, such as people accustomed to cursing others; the second, praising a person to receive benefit from him, and in that same praise he causes his enemy to stink, harming the one he is praising. The third, neither harmful nor beneficial, such as those accustomed to speak idle words and vain matters - how so-and-so's house was built, and how much it cost, and stories of kings and princes, and so on. The fourth, such as Torah and the Prophets, where lives depend on lives.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:56-: And there are among the sages of Torah those who divide these four into five parts: one, commanded; two, to be avoided; three, despised; four, beloved; five, permitted. One, commanded - such as speaking words of Torah and fear of the Name. Two, to be avoided - such as false testimony, gossip, and vulgar speech. Three, despised - having neither transgression nor much benefit, such as speaking of what has already happened, the customs of kings, and several matters of worldly affairs. And although the sage said that in this there is neither transgression nor benefit, another sage said there is transgression in it and no benefit. Four, the beloved - this is one who speaks in praise of good deeds and condemns evil deeds, and praises the righteous so that people improve their conduct in the eyes of others and follow their ways, and condemns the wicked so that they be despised and disdained in the eyes of others, and their memory erased, and people distance themselves from them and not conduct themselves as they do. Five, the permitted - this is speech of commerce and livelihood, to speak of clothing matters, of eating and drinking, and other needs - and whoever minimizes his words even in this matter is praiseworthy. And according to the words of the sages, most worldly talk has no need to be spoken.
Things that have a great prohibition to speak, such as mockery, flattery, and speaking slander - and concerning these four one should write a gate of its own for each.

In several places silence is good, such as if the attribute of judgment befalls him, as Aaron did, as it is said (Leviticus 10:3), "and Aaron was silent." And if a person hears his own disgrace and does not respond, this is a great commandment and a supernal virtue, to stay silent toward those who curse him. Also, a person shall train himself to be silent in the synagogue, and this is his modesty - and this requires great alacrity, to be silent in the synagogue and refrain from speaking even words of Torah, and all the more so other things, all so that he can direct his heart to prayer. And if he sits silently among friends and listens to their words, it is good when he is silent and hears what he did not know, while when he speaks he adds no knowledge - but if he is in doubt about the words of the Sages, he should ask them, for this silence is very bad.

King Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 3:7), "a time to be silent and a time to speak" - for sometimes silence is good, and sometimes speech is good. And the sage said, when you do not find a person to teach you discipline, cling to silence, lest you speak folly. Because the tongue is quick to speak, one must weigh down the tongue greatly and guard it so that it not multiply words, for a multitude of words is like a burden, and the heaviness of a multitude of words is heavier than the heaviness of much silence. If he hears that his fellow is speaking, he should stay silent until he finishes his words - and so Solomon said (Proverbs 18:13), "he who answers a matter before he hears it, it is folly and shame to him."

And whoever is accustomed to silence is saved from several transgressions - from curses and blasphemies, from slander, from mockery, from lies - for when a person is cursed and blasphemed by his fellow, if he answers him he shall multiply speech against him many times over. And so the sage said, I hear evil spoken against me, and I stay silent. They said to him, why? He said to them, if I answer my accuser, I fear that I shall hear other curses harsher than the first. And he said, when the fool argues with the wise man and the wise man stays silent, it is a great answer to the fool, for the fool is more distressed by the wise man's silence than if he had answered him - and concerning this it is said (Proverbs 26:4), "do not answer a fool according to his folly." And further, a person can reveal secrets to him, since he is not accustomed to a multitude of words and shall not reveal a secret - for a person does more with his tongue than with his sword, for a person stands here and delivers his fellow, distant from him, to death, but with a sword he can only kill one near him. Therefore man was created with two ears, two eyes, and two nostrils, and one mouth, to say that he should minimize his speech.

Silence is fitting for the wise, all the more so for fools (Pesachim 99a) - and "a fence for wisdom is silence." And sometimes silence is bad, as it is written (Proverbs 26:5), "answer a fool according to his folly" - concerning words of Torah, if you see that fools are casting their words upon words of Torah, answer them to correct their error. If a person sees another committing a transgression, he should protest with his hand and rebuke him - and Solomon already said (Proverbs 15:1), "a soft answer turns away wrath," and so on - therefore each person should train himself to have soft words and not be accustomed to harsh words.

And be careful with your tongue to guard it like the pupil of the eye, as it is said (ibid. 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles." If you sit in company, it is good that they say to you "speak" [rather than that you be reproached for staying silent] - but even if they curse you, it is better that you stay silent than that you speak, and your words become a burden to them.

And he should be very careful not to shame a person and not to cause distress with his words. If he sits near a person who has a blemish in his body of which he is ashamed, or has a blemish in his children or wife, or a flaw in his family, he should be very careful not to speak of that blemish or that flaw, even if he is not speaking about him but about another person who has this blemish, for he will always suppose that he is being spoken about and be ashamed.

If a person did something shameful and turned from it and repents, one should also be careful not to speak of that matter before him, or say to him, even in jest, "how could you have done such a thing, and why were you not careful about it?" - even this you should not do, for you shame him. If a person tells you words of Torah that you already know, be silent until he finishes the matter, for perhaps he will introduce something new that you did not know at first, and also he derives pleasure from telling you the matter - and even if you know that nothing new will come to you, be silent for him until he speaks and finishes.

Two people who had a quarrel with each other, and afterward made peace together - neither of them should say, "you did such-and-such to me, and therefore I did such-and-such to you," even if he has no intention of returning to their dispute - for from his saying "you did such-and-such to me," his fellow will answer, on the contrary, all the fault was yours - and from this the quarrel will be aroused again, and even if the quarrel is not aroused, the one at fault will be shamed.

One who sits before a sage and is silent has a reward, such as when he intends to listen. And there is one who is silent and has a transgression, such as when he thinks, what shall I say before him, since he does not know how to answer me properly, he certainly knows nothing compared to me. And he should be very careful concerning what our Rabbis said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 7), "seven things characterize a boor and seven a sage" - a sage does not speak before one greater than him in wisdom or in number, does not interrupt his fellow's words, is not rash to answer, answers the matter [asked] and asks according to the halachah, and speaks of the first matter first and the last matter last, and concerning what he has not heard says "I have not heard," and concedes to the truth - and the opposite of these in a boor. And the sage said, whoever speaks with wisdom and understanding is like salt in a dish, and there is grace in his fitting words upon his body, like settings of gold. "The wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded" (Ecclesiastes 9:16) - let him go to a person whose words are heeded and put his words in his mouth to make them heard, but he himself should stay silent.

The general rule of the matter is: just as a person makes a door for his entrance, and there is a time to close it and a time to open it, so he should close the doors of his mouth with the two doors of the lips and the teeth, and be very careful about opening your mouth, and guard your tongue as you would guard silver, gold, and pearls within your chamber and within your chests - and just as you make an enclosure for its enclosure, so you should do for your mouth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:68-: See how the early ones were careful about idle talk, that they would be praised for never having engaged in idle conversation all their days. And in this matter there is a great remedy for praying with intent, for most of the loss of intent in prayer comes from idle words fixed in one's heart. Also, silence is a great fence for the fear of Heaven, for it is impossible to be God-fearing with a heart that multiplies words.
And with this the chapter is concluded:

After we spoke, in the previous chapter, of the virtue of silence, we wish now, in this chapter, to explain the matter of the four groups that do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah, all of which depend on speech, as they said, of blessed memory, in Sotah (42a): Rav Chisda said, and some say Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba, four groups do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah - the group of scoffers, the group of flatterers, the group of liars, the group of slanderers - as it is written (Psalms 5:5), "for You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not sojourn with You." And in the Zohar they do not speak of these four groups together.

And it appears, as a general rule, that these blemish the four letters of Adonai, and therefore do not see the countenance of the Shechinah. And in blemishing any one group, it is a blemish to the whole Name, for the four letters are all one Name. And in blemishing the Shechinah, the secret of YHVH too withdraws from the Shechinah, and it is found that he cuts the unification - and therefore he does not see the countenance of the Shechinah. And the secret of the countenance of the Shechinah we shall further explain below.

And when you examine precisely, you shall find that each group blemishes one letter - the group of scoffers, the letter Alef, and the letter Yud, and so on - and therefore causes evil to himself and his soul, bringing sufferings upon him, for the reason that the supernal flow is diminished from its source, and likewise, from great heights he falls to the lowest depths in Gehinnom, and likewise his sustenance is diminished, for from there sustenance flows - "You open Your hand" (Psalms 145:16) - "Your hand [Yud-Dalet-Kaf]" (Tikkunei Zohar, page 7b) - meaning the withdrawal of His hand. The group of flatterers corresponds to Heh, because its essence is that he speaks one thing with his mouth and another with his heart, and the blemish is found in both together. The group of liars corresponds to Vav, for the Vav is the letter of truth, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 241b), concerning (Joshua 2:12), "and give me a true sign." The group of slanderers corresponds to the final Heh, and the teachings we shall write below prove this, and this is (Leviticus 14:2), "this shall be the law of the leper," and so on - and this is enough hint for the wise.

And I heard in the name of the Kabbalists that corresponding to these four groups are four impure animals: the rock badger, the hare, the camel, the pig. And corresponding to these there are four husks above to raise up the deed of the sinner and punish him in Gehinnom. And I further heard that whoever sinned and was of these four groups mentioned is destined to be reincarnated in the four impure animals, each one in the animal alluded to and corresponding to him.

And concerning the punishment of the mocker, Rabbi Elazar said (Avodah Zarah 18b): whoever mocks, sufferings come upon him, as it is said (Isaiah 28:22), "and now, do not mock," and so on, "for I have heard a decree of destruction," and so on. Rabbah said to the Rabbis, I beg of you, do not mock, so that sufferings not come upon you. Rav Ketina said, whoever mocks, his sustenance is diminished, as it is said (Hosea 7:5), "he stretched out his hand with mockers." And Rav Ketina said, whoever mocks falls into Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 21:24), "the proud, haughty one, scoffer is his name," and so on - and "wrath" [evrah] refers only to Gehinnom, as it is said (Zephaniah 1:15), "a day of wrath," and so on. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai said, whoever mocks causes destruction to the world, as it is said (Isaiah 28:22), "and now, do not mock," and so on, "for I have heard a decree of destruction." Rabbi Elazar said, mockery is harsh, for its beginning is sufferings and its end is destruction - to this point. Behold, it is explained how much evil it causes to himself, his soul, and the whole world.

And the master Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, letter 174) five divisions concerning the group of scoffers, in these words: mockery is harsh, for Jehu was not punished until he mocked, even though there was no deceit in his heart, as it is said (2 Kings 10:18), "and Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, Ahab served Baal a little," and so on. Mockery is harsh, for Scripture did not specify to expel anyone who commits transgressions except a scoffer, as it is said (Proverbs 22:10), "expel a scoffer, and strife shall depart." Mockery is harsh, for the punishment of the Flood generation did not come quickly until they mocked Noah, as it is said (Job 12:5), "the one at ease holds a torch in contempt," and so on - Noah was before them like a torch, and they held his words in contempt and mocked him. Mockery is harsh, for the punishment of Sodom did not come quickly until they mocked Lot, as it is said (Genesis 19:14), "and he seemed as one jesting in the eyes of his sons-in-law" - they said to him, fool, there are timbrels and flutes in the city, and you say it is being overturned! Mockery is harsh, for because of it forty-two men of Israel were killed, as it is said (2 Kings 2:23), "and young lads came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, go up, baldhead," and so on, and it is written, "and he turned around and saw them, and cursed them in the Name of the LORD." And Sanballat and Tobiah were punished only because they mocked Israel over the building of the Temple, as it is said (Nehemiah 2:19), "and Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite heard, and they mocked us." And for whoever mocks there is no remedy for his wound, as it is said (2 Chronicles 36:16), "and they mocked the messengers of God," and so on, "until the wrath of the LORD arose," and so on. And even in the lightest of light matters, a person is not permitted to mock, as it is said (Hosea 7:5), "he stretched out his hand with mockers."

And we read in Midrash Mishlei (Proverbs 9:12), "if you are wise, you are wise for yourself, and if you scoff, you alone shall bear it" - a parable of two people, one poor and one rich, and the poor one said to him, what benefit is there to a person from you? Everything you have acquired, you have acquired for yourself. So the Holy One, blessed be He, says to the wise man, although you have acquired wisdom, you have acquired it for yourself - therefore it is said, "if you are wise," and so on. Rabbi Elazar says, if you are wise in Torah, it is as though you gladden the Holy One, blessed be He, who gave it to you - as it is said, "you are wise for yourself" - for the One who gave you wisdom. "And if you scoff, you alone shall bear it" - and not others.

Further, they said, of blessed memory (Megillah 25b): all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry - from where do we learn this? From Elijah, of blessed memory, as it is said (1 Kings 18:27), "and it came to pass at noon, that Elijah mocked them," and so on. He said to them, the Baal you worship - does he have "siach" [a bush/complaint]? Did he perhaps create all the trees, as it is said (Genesis 2:5), "and every bush [siach] of the field"? Does he have "sig" [a border]? Did he perhaps establish all boundaries, as it is said (Deuteronomy 19:14), "you shall not move your neighbor's boundary"? Does he have "derech" [a way]? Did he perhaps split the sea for you and make a way in it, as it is said (Isaiah 43:16), "who gives a way in the sea"? "Perhaps he is asleep and will awaken" - or perhaps he revived your dead and awakens them from their sleep to the life of the World to Come? All these deeds are only the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He - it is fitting for Him to be served and worshipped, blessed be His Name forever and ever - to this point.

And concerning the essence of mockery, there are aspects to it. One of them is one who establishes himself at the corners [of the street] for idle talk and vain words, and this is called a scoffer - for they said in chapter 3 of Avot (mishnah 2), "two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers," and so on - and it says "who sit," even if they are not engaged in words of mockery, since there are no words of Torah between them it is called a session of scoffers - all the more so one occupied with idle talk, since he could occupy himself with Torah at that time and does not, he is called a scoffer.

And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz, peace be upon him, wrote concerning the reason for the matter, and said, in these words: and the reason is that the punishment for its neglect corresponds to the greatness of its reward, as it is said (Psalms 1:1), "and in the session of scoffers he has not sat" - and they said that the proof is from the end of the verse (ibid. 1:2), "but his desire is in the Torah of the LORD" - as though it said, because his desire is in the Torah of the LORD, he has not sat in the session of scoffers, which has no Torah of the LORD in it. And to me it is a complete proof from the verse he mentioned - is there a greater mockery than one to whom they said, count gold coins for one hour, and everything you count shall be yours, and he mocks the gold coins and disdains them? So too, one idle from words of Torah, after knowing this great reward, is nothing but a true scoffer. And so the sage said (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 2), "woe to the creatures for the insult to the Torah" - behold, he called one idle from the words of Torah an "insulter," and this is the intent here. And when the prophet Isaiah condemned the men of his generation who were idle from Torah, he called them "men of scoffing," as it is said (Isaiah 28:14), "hear the word of the LORD, you men of scoffing" - and this is a true indication concerning all these matters - to this point. And there is support for this in Tractate Sanhedrin (99a), where they said concerning "for he has despised the word of the LORD" - Rabbi Nechemiah says, whoever could occupy himself with Torah and does not, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:11-: And besides being called a scoffer, one who speaks idle words also transgresses a positive commandment, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:7), "and you shall speak of them" - and so in Tractate Yoma, first chapter (19b), in these words: our Rabbis taught, "and you shall speak of them" - and not in prayer. "Of them" you have permission to speak, and not of other matters. "And you shall speak of them" - make them fixed. Rava said, whoever engages in idle conversation transgresses a positive commandment, as it is said, "and you shall speak of them," and not of other matters. Rav Acha bar Yaakov said, he transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 1:8), "all things are wearisome, man cannot speak [of them all]" - to this point, their wording.

And especially students of Torah must be very careful of idle words, for they said in the Midrash Shir HaShirim Rabbah (1:21), on the verse (1:3), "for the fragrance of your good oils" - in these words: what is oil like? A full cup does not overflow with other liquids [as easily], so words of Torah do not overflow with words of mockery. Just as with this oil, if a cup full of oil is in your hand and a drop of water falls into it, a drop of oil comes out to match it - so if a word of Torah enters the heart, a word of mockery comes out to match it; if a word of mockery enters the heart, a word of Torah comes out to match it - to this point.

And included in this group is the group who play dice and other kinds of games - even if they do not play to win money from each other, which would involve theft, there is still the matter of "two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers," as explained. And this resembles the kinds of games mentioned in Tractate Avodah Zarah (18b), where they said that they are a session of scoffers, in these words: our Rabbis taught, whoever goes to the stadiums or the circuses and sees there the snake-charmers, the buffoons, the masked performers, the tumblers, the acrobats, the [various entertainers] - this is a session of scoffers, and concerning them Scripture says (Psalms 1:1), "who has not walked," and so on, "but whose desire is in the Torah of the LORD" - from this you learn that these things bring a person to the nullification of Torah - to this point. And Rashi explains "bukyon," and so on, as kinds of mockery - from this you learn, from its being juxtaposed with "but... in the Torah," that whoever goes to these does not desire the Torah of the LORD - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that since he is idle from the Torah of the LORD in these kinds of games, they are called a session of scoffers - and the same applies to other kinds of games.

And there are those who have permitted themselves games of dice, saying that it is something that sharpens the mind - and I saw fit to expose their error, so that they not become clever with arguments of their own inclination against the Torah of the LORD. First, what Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sefer HaYirah, that one who speaks idle words is like one who denies the fundamental principle, for he does not believe that the whole earth is full of His glory - for one who believes that he stands before the blessed and exalted King would not do anything against His will. And in my eyes this matter is more difficult than all other transgressions - for with all other transgressions, if the sinner sins momentarily, suddenly led astray by his inclination and not placing the fear of the LORD before him, his punishment is not so great; but this one, who with contempt of soul sits an hour or three hours, and sometimes the whole day, does not remember the LORD before him, and does not say in his heart, before whom do I stand and play, stand and provoke - and is not ashamed before His greatness and does not fear His judgment, and transgresses the negative commandment "take heed to yourself, lest you forget the LORD your God" - he forgets the LORD, and even so sits and plays - behold, he willfully disgraces the LORD and His Torah, saying in his heart that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not punish the group of scoffers - and he denies the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and is a Sadducee. He resembles those about whom the Holy One, blessed be He, complained to the prophet Ezekiel, who worshipped idols in secret and said (Ezekiel 8:12), "the LORD has forsaken the land, the LORD does not see us" - and these worship idols openly, meaning they give an excuse as though it were permitted to do so publicly, with no one protesting against them. And if our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Nedarim 22b) of one who becomes angry, that the Shechinah is not significant in his eyes, all the more so should this be said of this group, as explained.

And further, we find in the Talmud (Niddah 13a) concerning one who holds his member while urinating, that they said to Rabbi Eliezer that he appeared to have a crushed member and thus cast an aspersion on his children, that they were illegitimate - and he answered, better that he cast an aspersion on his children, that they are illegitimate, than that he make himself a wicked man before the Omnipresent for even one moment. And along these lines, all the more so, one who plays dice, making himself wicked before the Omnipresent for more than two hours, and possibly the whole day - this argument is one of reason.

And further, in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, they said in Tractate Bava Batra (79a): Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, whoever separates himself from words of Torah and occupies himself with idle conversation, fire consumes him, as it is said (Ezekiel 15:7), "and I will set My face against them; they shall go out from the fire, but the fire shall consume them." Further there, when Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, whoever weakens himself from the words of Torah falls into Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 21:16), "a man who strays from the way of understanding shall rest in the assembly of the departed [refa'im]" - and "refa'im" refers only to those who descend to Gehinnom, as it is said (ibid. 9:18), "but he does not know that the departed are there, in the depths of Sheol," and so on - to this point.

And Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor (letter 31), in these words: and one who occupies himself with idle matters, even if there is no forbidden speech in it, loses the time he could have occupied with words of Torah to acquire the life of the World to Come - and it appears from his mind that he disdains the words of the Name and the reward of the World to Come, as we read in the chapter "Chelek" (99a): it was taught, Rabbi Meir says, whoever learns Torah and does not teach it, this is "for he has despised the word of the LORD"; Rabbi Nehorai says, whoever could occupy himself with Torah and does not - to this point.

And not only that, but even one who could occupy himself with Torah and does not wish to, even if he does not speak words of mockery, his session is called a session of scoffers, as we learned in chapter 3 of Avot, "two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers," and so on. And it is not enough that he sins against his own soul and loses the life of the World to Come and inherits Gehinnom, but he also causes the multitude to sin - for by occupying himself with idle conversation he draws the heart of the multitude to be idle with him, and their sin depends on him, as we learned in chapter 5 of Avot, "Jeroboam sinned and caused the multitude to sin, the sin of the multitude is dependent on him," as it is said (2 Kings 13:2), "because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and caused Israel to sin." And they also punish him by not giving him the means to repent, than which there is no greater punishment, as we read in the chapter "Yom HaKippurim" (Yoma 87a): whoever gives merit to the multitude, no sin comes through him; and whoever causes the multitude to sin is not given the means to repent - to this point, relevant here.

And let not the speaker say, who can be careful to keep all the words of our Rabbis, so I shall be careful now about this one - and since he is not careful about the others, he shall not be careful about this one either. This argument too is rejected, for one transgression drags another (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 2), and if he is not careful about this one, his inclination will bring him to sin in all four groups that do not see the countenance of the Shechinah, in a manner that he shall be excluded from the World to Come - and woe to him who says with his mouth that he does not wish to see the countenance of the Shechinah, in order to fulfill the will of his inclination and be among the group of scoffers and the other groups. But if he sanctifies himself in this one, "whoever comes to be purified is assisted" (Yoma 38b), and he shall not sin in the other groups and shall be saved from them, as they said, of blessed memory (Yoma 39a), "a person who sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him much."

And those who play dice and other kinds of games on festivals and appointed times, woe to their souls, for they have done themselves harm - for the days of the appointed times are days of judgment, as they said, of blessed memory (Rosh Hashanah, chapter 1, mishnah 1), "at four points the world is judged: on Passover, concerning the grain; on Shavuot [Atzeret], concerning the fruit of the tree; on Rosh Hashanah, all who come into the world pass before Him like a flock; on Sukkot, they are judged concerning water." Behold, all the appointed times are days of judgment, and therefore they said (Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 15, halachah 3) that Sabbaths and festivals were given to Israel only so that they occupy themselves with Torah. And they said (Kiddushin 40b), "a person should always view himself and the world as half meritorious and half guilty; if he does one meritorious deed, happy is he, for he has tipped himself and the whole world to the scale of merit, and if not, Heaven forfend, he has tipped it to the scale of guilt." It follows that a sinner then, in play and levity, is more severe than at other times of the year - for since the world is in judgment, through one sin the world might be tipped to the scale of guilt, and then all those poor who die or suffer from the poverty of hunger and thirst are all dependent on him.

And on the days of the appointed times, besides a person's sustenance depending on it, a person's life and soul also depend on judgment, and so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in his explanation of this Mishnah that we copied (Zohar, Parashat Vayechi, page 226b), that it all speaks of the souls being judged - see there.

And therefore it is fitting to distance oneself from all kinds of games, whether on weekdays or on the days of the appointed times, for the world and man are always in judgment, as we copied the teachings of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Parashat Vayechi, pages 226b-227a), and the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Rosh Hashanah 16a), in the Gate of Fear, chapter 11. And this sin causes sufferings and destruction to the world, according to the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Avodah Zarah 18b) - therefore one must be careful not to stumble further, and his repentance shall be accepted, with God's help.

And it appears that all those explanations stated there (Sanhedrin 99a), explaining the verse "for he has despised the word of the LORD," are all included in mockery, for the mocker is the one who disdains matters, as we have said. It says there: "for he has despised the word of the LORD" (Numbers 15:31) - this is one who says the Torah is not from Heaven. Another interpretation: this is a heretic. "And has broken His commandment" - this is one who breaks the covenant of the flesh. It was taught in another [teaching]: "for he has despised the word of the LORD" - this is one who says the Torah is not from Heaven; and even if he said the whole Torah is from Heaven except for this verse, that not the Holy One, blessed be He, but Moses said it of his own accord - this is "for he has despised the word of the LORD"; and even if he said the whole Torah is from Heaven except for this fine point, this a fortiori argument, this verbal analogy - this is "for he has despised the word of the LORD." It was taught: Rabbi Meir would say, whoever learns Torah and does not teach it, this is "for he has despised the word of the LORD." Rabbi Natan says, whoever does not pay attention to the Mishnah. Rabbi Nechemiah says, and so on - to this point, relevant here.
